rv.q: Grandage’s production oozes sensory pleasure...this is theatre to make the heart leap: a blazing beacon to progress, to possibility, to freedom and the power of imagination.
It couldn't feel more timely, and it's glorious.

A captivating Corrin – a timeless, ageless pixie with a shock of white hair – inhabits the role to perfection, combining the dash and dazzle of a kingfisher with the casual sense of entitlement of an aristo.
You're ever in the presence of pure star quality.
A larky, optimistic evening fully exploiting Corrin's magnetism but one that's Rizla-thin.
It feels like commercial and art-house theatre are productively entwined here, bringing a questing intelligence and star power to hot-button issues.
This is a fantastic performance, full of gentle detail – shoulders wriggling in distaste, eyes wide in discovery – and Corrin provides the compelling heart of a problematic play.
Performances and design of unique warmth and wit create an outstandingly original theatrical pleasure.
This is a giddy and enthralling production of a unique story that feels like a breath of fresh air.
Emma Corrin's Orlando is the shining centre of this delightful production with Deborah Findlay a great comic presence as earthy Mrs Grimsditch.
A flawed but engaging experiment, and one given a beating heart by the magnificent, mercurial Corrin.
I love Virginia Woolf, this is an interesting reflection on the novel... while I am left wanting more emotional oomph, I did enjoy this.
What Orlando lacks is content, so while this nifty production races through the centuries, Orlando spends most of it in bed.

There is enough flair and wit in this slick production to convey some sense of Woolf’s wildly original vision...when the frenzied flow of time is finally arrested at its close, this 'Orlando' leaves one wanting much more.
It's clear what the plays intentions are, but it never comes close to realising them.
Although it looks sensational, it's an eccentric triviality aimed at 1970s feminists.
Neil Bartlett's version somehow felt a bit disappointing: insubstantial though witty and mischievous.
It is absolutely wonderful and as much a love letter to theatre as a joyful interrogation of sex, gender and love.
